en: Question him closely.
Ask what will become of the people
And what danger Ezkara intends.
Ask where Almambet, Chubak,
And the hero Manas have gone;
From the snarling Chinese,
My precious kinsman Sarykan,
Demand an answer!”
When Külchoro had spoken thus,
The bloodthirsty warrior came forth prepared;
Khan Bakay, my khan and elder, stepped forward
And pleaded with Külchoro:
“For a son like you,
I, your elder Bakay, would gladly sacrifice myself!
Ah, my champion Külchoro,
If you lead this great onslaught,
Capture Kongurbay,
And give us that spectacle,
Then in Bakay’s old age
I shall present you from my herds
My treasured beast Kökcholok.
If that provision is too little,
Pour my blood into a leather flask and take it;
If need be, Külchoro,
Take your elder’s very life.
Charge straight at the brooding Kongurbay
And thrust your spear into him;
Free my soul
From this grievous hell of torment.
Charge upon the swaggering Kalmyk
And drive your spear through him;
For the sake of the great Kyrgyz nation,
Cut the throat of the infidel
Who mines the veins of gold.
From the vast nation of China’s forty tribes,
Avenge the Kyrgyz.
What lion is fit for such a feat?
A hero like you is fit for combat.
Strike the black-worm infidels
With a mighty blow.
My dear Külchoro,
A lion like you is fit for such a feat;
Avenge the bloodthirsty heroes of old.
You have always been resourceful and lionhearted;
I believed you would spread slaughter across the world—
My dear one, you alone were my hope.
For God’s sake and mine,
And for the people left by your one father,
Spare nothing—deal out slaughter.
On Alööke’s son Kongurbay,
Take vengeance as one would upon a dog.”
Thus spoke Khan Bakay:
“The khan himself will be your opponent;
Only a lord of immense courage is fit
For that fierce and bloody battle.
My Külchoro, it calls for a lion like you.
My spring flowing down from the hills,
My colt whom I fondly raised,
Knowing he would one day serve in vengeance.”
After Bakay had spoken thus,
The gray-maned warrior of old said:
“Against grim-faced Kongurbay,
That doomed Kalmyk warrior,
Let us unleash a storm of gunfire.
Let us empty the bullets from our powder flasks
And stand amid the thunder of the guns.
Let us stand face-to-face,
Shouting as we thrust our spears,
Firing muskets and drawing bows,
Clashing fiercely in combat;
Let us wage war in earnest.
Until the soft reeds ripen,
Until the ashes of the steppe grass fly,
Until the birches shed their covering,
And the poplars lose every leaf,
Let us wage war in this fashion.
Let us begin the clash with fury;
Let us leave sixty young wives widowed
And their villages desolate.
In broad Beijing, once conquered by our fathers,
Let us open fire and begin the slaughter.
With our bearded elder Bakay,
Let us all enter the fray—
Can one who fears death prosper?
Can a soul that recoils from its destined end
Prosper as a man?
My companion, one of seven days brings death;
When doom arrives, who does not die?
If Almighty Allah wills it,
Will one not surrender one’s tiny life?
Will not the five-fingered angel reach out?
When the naked devourer of souls
Draws near to one’s life,
Will it not lower one into the dug grave,
And sink one beneath the black earth?
Can one who fears death prosper?
Can there ever be two brave men
Who turn back from their destined end?
Damn you, Kulchoro,
Lionhearted companion sustained by the spirits—
A warrior whose swiftness knows no bounds,
A dashing, vigorous companion!
Kulchoro, when I first saw you,
We swiftly invoked Baabedin,
And for what I had newly received,
We quickly recited the ayat.
Exactly ninety-five red camels
Were slaughtered for the feast;
Minstrels were made to sing,
And judges of men to appraise you,
While an amulet was hung around your neck.
“He will become a peerless sultan,” they said.
My khan father’s confidant,
Dear Bakai, his old companion,
With sixty khojas and forty ishans,
All examined you and gave their blessing.
They had a golden cradle brought,
And, wishing you to become an exceptional man,
They placed you in that cradle.
Kulchoro, raised with loving care,
You are the companion I made my cherished one.
My companion, favored by perfect fortune,
Dark within and blue-gray without,
My peerless heroic companion.
Your eyes have seen a thousand roads;
Believing they would one day serve a great need,
I cherished and raised you myself.
I slaughtered ninety beasts for your feast;
I gave you a fitting name
So that you might subdue every foe you faced
And crush him into the earth.
Thinking to feed the children,
I had young mares slaughtered.
The honeyed fat of those mares
I cut for you with my teeth
And made you suck from my tongue.
Fearing the wind and breeze would touch you,
I had you covered with a fine veil;
Fearing you might defer to another,
I raised you wild and headstrong
And let you heed no one’s word.
I chose the finest brisket and rump fat
And fed them to you.
Among the countless Argyn and Kyrgyz,
Who could ever call you a mere child?
For a champion son like you,
Your precious elder would sacrifice himself.
When I dwell in the Ala-Too
And settle beside a river,
If my belly grows hungry,
I cut off rump fat and eat.
If my Külchoro is beside me,
I think, ‘I shall destroy the Jiangjun.’
When my belly grows hungry,
I cut off rich belly fat and eat;
While I have my treasured companion,
I think, ‘Let alone China,
O my colt, I shall spread slaughter
Across the whole world.’
If I stroke Taibuurul’s tail
And race the steed afar,
I think, ‘My horse will return victorious.’
If my mountain-sized Külchoro
Stands shouting beside me,
I think, ‘Let alone China,
I can make my claim against the whole world.’
With the black sword Zulpukor,
I think, ‘I shall cut them down,’
So long as my beloved companion lives;
Against the whole wide world
I think, ‘I shall drive my way through.’
With the red sword Zulpukor,
I think, ‘I shall cut them down.’
I have a musket before me
And many enemies who oppose me.
I shall storm in and crush them;
So long as my beloved companion lives,
I think, ‘I shall become a khan.’
If my Külchoro remains true,
I shall become a mountain pass,
Lofty and towering
Like the Ala-Too.
My fame spreading throughout the world,
I think, ‘I shall become a lion.’
If I contend with the khan,
I used to say, ‘I know how to hew him down.’
The Chinese and Manchus who grapple with me,
By sheer force
I think, ‘I know how to drive them back.’
The khan himself is my opponent;
I shall strike again and make them swarm,
Spill their blood and subdue them.
Those who heed words
I shall persuade and subdue;
Those brutes who understand no words
I shall bring to the faith and subdue.
Through the soaring Kara-Too
And along the lower reaches of the Kars River,
I intend to make a road.
The vast Chinese city of Beijing—
I stand ready to bring them low.
The true sovereign of the Khagan,
I stand ready to take his land,
And all the forty tribes
Upon the face of the earth.
For the lionhearted, magnanimous hero
I once vowed to take revenge.
If the Chinese flee in terror,
From the mouth of Keng-Jailak,
From the mountain of the golden mine,
I vowed to seize their land,
And avenge Almambet, Chubak, and Syrgak.
I vowed to settle their blood feud.
I will break through Beijing’s frontier
And proclaim, “This is Kyrgyz land,”
And raise up a khan.
After crushing the Khagan’s realm,
I intend, when Bakai has grown old,
To raise him as khan
Over the countless Chinese and their khagan.
Wheeling about and battling,
Shouting and thrusting spears,
When we turn upon the Khagan
I mean to bring him ruin.
When Kongurbay faces us,
If valiant Külchoro’s aim is true,
I mean to give him a spectacle.
The sands blaze and shimmer there;
If a cauldron is set upon the sand,
It roars and boils over.
No living creature
That encounters it survives.
Haze rises, gathering at the corners,
And dust billows through the hollows and ridges.
I will encircle the Chinese
And seize their land.
From the forty khans of teeming China
I mean to capture their armies.
From among Ulungtu’s sons,
From the mountains of Great Kaspan,
The perilous Kara-Suu—
This is the ill-fated place
Of which the ancients spoke.
From the plain of Kara-Suu,
From the mouth of Tash-Kapchal,
In the mountains of Kaspan-Tau,
There is a treasury of gold mines;
I intend to take its ore.
Kara-Tau, from which the forty Chinese tribes
Of Beijing obtain their tea—
That towering, lofty mountain—
I intend to take its land.
Wearing motley trousers and blue shirts,
Black caps and baggy breeches,
The many Chinese who look like women—
I intend to take their people.
